KEY MESSAGE 1...As of 1:55 PM EDT...Current sfc analysis shows 
a 1024 mb sfc high centered over southeast PA, while visible 
satellite imagery is showing some fair-weather cumulus clouds 
across the region. Temperatures should run near to slightly 
below normal this afternoon with highs in the mid to upper 70s 
and low humidity, making for a very nice Saturday afternoon. 
While the sfc high begins to slide off to the east tonight, 
temperatures should initially drop quickly after sunset, 
although increasing high clouds especially after midnight will 
keep lows a few degrees warmer than last night for most areas. 
It will still be a very comfortable night with temperatures 
mostly in the 50s, except for some 40s in the higher elevations.
Patchy fog is possible in some of the typical river valley 
areas as well. 

Tomorrow, an upper-level shortwave approaching from the west and
a low-level warm front approaching from the southwest will lead
to further increasing clouds as well as some scattered showers 
and a few thunderstorms, mainly during the afternoon. NBM has 
been slow to catch up to the CAM guidance, so we increased PoPs 
into the slight chance to chance category across most of the 
region tomorrow afternoon and evening. The best chance for 
showers or a storm appears to be across the eastern Catskills 
and Mid Hudson Valley. While deep-layer shear is decent at 
>30-35 kt, instability looks fairly limited with only up to ~500
J/kg per the latest HREF. Warm temperatures aloft will and 
meager mid-level lapse rates will further limit the threat for 
severe weather. Some additional showers and a few storms are 
possible late Monday evening into Monday night in association 
with another upper disturbance that will push the frontal 
boundary back to our south and west as a cold front. Best chance
for showers and a few storms will remain for the Mid Hudson 
Valley and Catskills, with the rest of the region drying out as 
a ridge of sfc high pressure builds down from the north. Some 
additional patchy fog will be possible, especially for areas 
that see rain tomorrow afternoon/evening. 

Monday looks to be the last tranquil day across the region. The 
ridge of sfc high pressure should help keep the frontal boundary 
well to our southwest through the day, with model forecast soundings 
suggesting abundant mid-level dry air and a capping inversion that 
will keep our region dry through at least the evening, although 
shower chances increase Monday night as the boundary lifts back 
north as a warm front. Temperatures Sunday and Monday will be in the 
upper 70s to low 80s for valley areas. 


KEY MESSAGE 2...The long term period will be dominated by a closed 
upper ridge centered near Tennessee, placing much of the Northeast 
in fast W/NW flow aloft. Multiple shortwave disturbances are 
expected to track around the periphery of the upper ridge over our 
region. This will lead to several chances for showers and 
thunderstorms through the week, and some may be strong to severe if 
1) the aforementioned frontal boundary remains close enough to 
our region and 2) the timing of these disturbances aligns with 
peak diurnal heating...

As the boundary lifts north as a warm front Monday night into 
Tuesday, the first upper shortwave will track into our region. There 
remains some questions as to the exact position of the warm front 
and timing of this disturbance, but there is surprisingly good 
agreement in the numerical guidance at this lead time for an MCS or 
decaying MCS to track into our region Monday night or Tuesday. If 
this system is a little slower and arrives Tuesday late morning or 
early afternoon, then there may be enough instability for some 
stronger storms as forcing looks quite strong and deep-layer shear 
is expected to be rather impressive at >40 kt. PWATs also increase 
to 1-2 std dev above normal per the NAEFS, so some locally heavy 
rain is also possible especially along the edges of any potential 
MCS where there is a better chance for training. WPC has placed our 
region in the D3 and D4 marginal risk ERO, but will note that the D3 
inclusion is really for late Monday night as most of the day Monday 
will be dry.

For Wednesday through Thursday, confidence is lower, but the pattern 
remains conducive for additional shower and storm chances. AI/ML 
guidance continues to highlight Wednesday as having the best 
potential for severe weather, especially from I-90 south and west. 
SPC has placed this area in the equivalent of a slight risk for 
severe weather. However, this will largely depend on the position of 
the frontal boundary. Some sources of guidance (GFS) have an area of
